insight.title: Google SRE monitoring: page symptoms, diagnose causes
insight.one_liner: Reliable monitoring separates user-visible symptoms from internal causes, uses black-box and white-box signals for different jobs, and protects human attention with simple low-noise paging rules.
insight.why_this_matters: More telemetry does not automatically create better operations. The SRE model is a decision system: detect meaningful service impact, keep paging simple and scarce, use internal signals for diagnosis, and start service coverage with latency, traffic, errors and saturation rather than indiscriminate metric volume.

whole_source_map.problem: Monitoring systems can collect vast internal data yet still fail operators by paging on noise, hiding user-visible impact, or mixing detection of what is broken with diagnosis of why it is broken.
whole_source_map.thesis: Use black-box monitoring for externally visible symptoms, white-box monitoring for internal diagnosis/imminent failures, four golden signals as a compact baseline, and simple high-signal pager rules because human interruption is expensive.

derived_model.problem: Telemetry volume and alert sophistication can increase while operator awareness gets worse because low-value alerts compete with real failures for attention.
derived_model.mechanism: Anchor detection in service symptoms, retain white-box internal visibility for diagnosis and imminent/masked issues, watch the four golden signals, and route only simple actionable conditions to a pager.
derived_model.result: Operators receive fewer higher-value interruptions while still retaining enough internal telemetry to explain causes and perform retrospective debugging.

central_chain: Monitoring serves several purposes, but paging has the strictest requirement because it interrupts a human.
A symptom answers what users experience; a cause explains why the symptom exists and should not be confused with the paging condition itself.
Black-box monitoring observes externally visible behavior and is strong for ongoing user-impact symptoms.
White-box monitoring exposes internal system behavior and is essential for diagnosis plus masked or imminent failures.
Latency, traffic, errors and saturation provide a compact baseline, while pager rules stay simple, robust and low-noise.
open_gaps: The chapter's paging model predates later burn-rate/SLO alerting practices that should be sourced separately.
The four golden signals are a service-health baseline, not a complete integrity/security/business-correctness model.

dominant.title: Detect impact first, diagnose cause second

nodes.label: 01 · Observe
nodes.title: Black-box symptom
nodes.text: Measure what users can actually experience: availability, latency, errors or lost capacity.

nodes.label: 02 · Decide
nodes.title: Is a human needed?
nodes.text: Page only when the condition is real, important and actionable enough to justify interruption.

nodes.label: 03 · Diagnose
nodes.title: White-box cause
nodes.text: Use internal metrics, logs and traces to explain the symptom or expose masked failures.

nodes.label: 04 · Improve
nodes.title: Reduce future noise
nodes.text: Fix root causes and simplify monitoring so pages remain scarce and trustworthy.

image.reason: The distinction between symptom-driven paging and internal diagnosis is an operational sequence, not an illustration problem.

concepts.name: Black-box monitoring
concepts.why_needed: Externally visible behavior gives the strongest evidence that a user-impacting problem is actually happening.

concepts.name: White-box monitoring
concepts.why_needed: Internal instrumentation is required to diagnose causes and detect masked or imminent failures.

concepts.name: Four golden signals
concepts.why_needed: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation form a compact default vocabulary for service health.

concepts.name: Actionable paging
concepts.why_needed: Human interruption is expensive, so pager rules must optimize for signal and actionability rather than telemetry coverage.

examples.scenario: Database retries hide intermittent backend errors and users still receive successful responses.
examples.question: Should this page the frontend team now, or remain a white-box diagnostic/imminent-risk signal until a real service symptom appears?

examples.scenario: Users see high latency while database read time also rises.
examples.question: Which measurement establishes the service symptom and which helps diagnose the cause without confusing the two?

examples.scenario: A team has hundreds of metrics but responders ignore frequent alerts.
examples.question: Which latency/traffic/error/saturation signals correspond to real impact, and which rules should become dashboards or tickets rather than pages?

limitations: The four golden signals do not replace domain-specific correctness, security, data-integrity or business-process monitoring.
Black-box monitoring is weak for not-yet-visible failures; internal white-box signals remain necessary for prediction and diagnosis.
White-box monitoring can create alert noise when internal anomalies page humans without demonstrated service impact.
Complex dependency-aware alerting can be fragile as systems change; the chapter explicitly favors a simple and comprehensible critical pager path.

use_now: For every page, write the user/service symptom it represents and the action expected from the responder; demote rules that cannot answer both.
Separate detection dashboards from diagnostic telemetry instead of requiring every collected signal to generate an alert.
try: Map one service to latency, traffic, errors and saturation, then label each existing alert as black-box symptom, white-box cause, ticket or page.
build: A small monitoring review worksheet that classifies each alert by symptom/cause, black/white box, actionability and human-interruption cost.
watch: Whether low-severity internal signals are silently drifting back into pager paths and reducing trust in alerts.
ignore_for_now: Complex causal/dependency alert hierarchies that are harder to understand than the service failure they are meant to detect.

connections: observability: this source refines generic telemetry into an operator decision model with different roles for detection, diagnosis and paging
distributed-trace: tracing is one white-box mechanism that helps explain a distributed cause but does not define whether a human should be paged

concepts.label: Black-box monitoring
concepts.summary: Monitoring externally visible service behavior as a user would experience it, emphasizing active symptoms and impact rather than internal implementation state.

concepts.label: White-box monitoring
concepts.summary: Monitoring internal system metrics, logs or interfaces to diagnose causes and expose masked or imminent failures not visible from the outside.

concepts.label: Four golden signals
concepts.summary: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation used as a compact baseline set of service-health signals for user-facing systems.

concepts.label: Actionable paging
concepts.summary: Restricting human-interrupting alerts to simple, high-signal conditions representing real or imminent problems that warrant direct operator action.

relations.rationale: Black-box symptoms and white-box internal signals answer complementary questions about service impact and diagnosis rather than replacing one another.
The chapter gives black-box symptom monitoring a key role in paging because it forces attention toward problems that are already affecting externally visible behavior.
Latency, traffic, errors and saturation provide a compact service-health baseline that can anchor symptom-oriented monitoring and dashboards.
